Deep learning · chapter 2.4c · object detection and 3D vision

Object Detection, 3D Vision & Vision Applications

From “what is in this picture?” to “where is it, how far away, and what should I do about it?”

A classifier gives one label per photo. Real uses of vision need more: a box around every object, the distance to each surface, the pose of each person, a sentence that matches the picture, a brake pedal pressed in time. This chapter builds those skills one by one, on real data: a published detector’s raw output on COCO photographs, and a calibrated stereo pair from the ETH3D benchmark. Touch the figure: in Detect, move over the photo to see what one cell of the detector’s grid predicts; in Rebuild in 3D, drag to turn a scene that this page reconstructs from two photographs.

The task

From labels to boxes: what, and where

Deep learning took over computer vision in 2012, when a convolutional network (Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton) cut the top-5 error of the ImageNet challenge to 15.3%, against 26.2% for the best entry built on hand-made features. Three years later residual networks were at 3.57%. The same networks, trained on large labelled sets, then spread to every vision task with a clear input and output: finding objects, segmenting them, estimating depth and pose, describing scenes. Their strength is the one met in the CNN chapters: features are learned, not designed, and convolution shares them across positions.

Classification answers what. An object detector answers what and where: it returns a list of (class, box, score) triples, one per object, however many there are. A box is four numbers, (x₁, y₁) for the top-left corner and (x₂, y₂) for the bottom-right. To grade a predicted box against a hand-drawn one we need a single overlap number, and the standard one is intersection over union. A detection counts as correct when its IoU with a box of the same class passes a threshold: 0.5 in the older PASCAL VOC benchmark; COCO averages over ten thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, so it rewards tight boxes. Drag the two corners of the dashed box on this real COCO photo, and move the threshold.

\[ \text{IoU}(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|} = \frac{I}{|A| + |B| - I} \]
Read it as: I is the area where the two boxes overlap and |A|, |B| are their own areas. The union counts the overlap only once, so it is |A| + |B| − I. IoU is 1 for identical boxes and 0 for boxes that do not touch. It does not care about absolute size: a 10-pixel shift costs a small box far more than a large one.
Say it“IoU is the overlap area over the union area: I over A plus B minus I.”

Two-stage detectors

Region proposals: decide where to look, then look

The oldest recipe is the sliding window: run a classifier on every window of every size and shape, and keep the windows it likes. That is a lot of windows, and nearly all of them are background. The fix is a cheap first stage that proposes a few thousand boxes likely to hold something, followed by an expensive second stage that classifies each proposal and tightens its box. R-CNN (Girshick et al., 2014) took about 2,000 proposals from a hand-made grouping algorithm and ran a whole CNN on each one; Fast R-CNN ran the CNN once and cut each proposal’s features out of the shared feature map (RoI pooling resamples that crop to a fixed grid, say 7 × 7, so a fixed-size head can read it).

Faster R-CNN (Ren et al., 2015) made the proposals learned too. Its region proposal network places a set of reference boxes, anchors, at every position of the feature map: 3 sizes × 3 aspect ratios = 9 per position. For each anchor it predicts an objectness score and four numbers that nudge the anchor onto the object. During training an anchor is a positive example if its IoU with some object is at least 0.7 (or it is that object’s best anchor), a negative if its IoU with every object is below 0.3, and ignored in between. Drag the anchor centre over the photo and watch the nine anchors change label; then jump to the best anchor for the chosen object.

\[ \begin{aligned} t_x &= \frac{x - x_a}{w_a}, & t_y &= \frac{y - y_a}{h_a} \\ t_w &= \ln\frac{w}{w_a}, & t_h &= \ln\frac{h}{h_a} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: (xa, ya, wa, ha) is the anchor’s centre, width and height; (x, y, w, h) is the object’s box. The network learns to output these four targets. Shifts are measured in units of the anchor’s own size and sizes on a log scale, so the same numbers mean the same thing for a tiny anchor and a huge one. Inverting them, x = xa + txwa and w = waetw, turns a prediction back into a box.
Say it“t-x is the shift over the anchor width; t-w is the log of the width ratio; the same for y and height.”

Single pass

One-stage detectors, and cleaning up with NMS

One-stage detectors drop the proposal stage. YOLO (Redmon et al., 2016) split the image into a grid and let every cell predict boxes, an objectness score and class probabilities, all in one forward pass; SSD (Liu et al., 2016) did the same on several feature maps of different resolution, so small objects are found on fine grids and large ones on coarse grids. They are fast enough for video, and in later versions about as accurate as two-stage models.

Everything below comes from a real one: YOLOX-Nano (Ge et al., 2021), a 0.9-million-parameter, anchor-free detector. At a 416 × 416 input it has three grids, 52 × 52 cells at stride 8, 26 × 26 at stride 16 and 13 × 13 at stride 32: 3,549 predictions per image. It was run offline on these photos with ONNX Runtime; the page holds its raw outputs and does the decoding, thresholding and suppression itself. Because neighbouring cells all see the same object, one object produces a cluster of overlapping boxes. Non-maximum suppression keeps the best box of each cluster and deletes the rest. Slide the score threshold and the NMS overlap and count true and false detections.

\[ \begin{aligned} c_x &= (g_x + t_x)\,s, & w &= s\,e^{t_w} \\ \text{score} &= p_{\text{obj}} \cdot \max_k p(k) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the cell at column gx of a grid with stride s pixels predicts an offset tx from its own corner, so the box centre lands near that cell; the width is the stride scaled by etw (and the same for y and h). The score multiplies “there is an object here” by the probability of the best class.
Say it“Centre x is cell plus offset, times the stride; width is the stride times e to the t-w; score is objectness times the best class probability.”
\[ \begin{aligned} &b^\ast = \arg\max_{b \in \mathcal B} \text{score}(b) \\ &\mathcal B \leftarrow \{\, b \in \mathcal B : \text{IoU}(b, b^\ast) \le \theta \,\} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: greedy NMS. Take the highest-scoring box b* left in the set, keep it, and delete every remaining box of the same class that overlaps it by more than θ. Repeat until the set is empty. A low θ can delete a true neighbour (two people side by side); a high θ leaves duplicates, each of which counts as a false positive.
Say it“Keep the best box, drop everything that overlaps it by more than theta, repeat.”

3D from two views

Two eyes: depth from disparity

A photograph flattens the world: every point along a ray from the camera lands on the same pixel, so depth is lost. Several cues bring it back, and the strongest is a second view. If we know where the two cameras are, and we can find the same scene point in both images (the correspondence problem), the two rays through it cross at exactly one place. Finding the match is the hard part, and geometry makes it easier: the match of a pixel must lie on a single line in the other image, its epipolar line. After rectification, which warps both images as if the cameras were side by side and parallel, that line is simply the same row.

Then depth comes from one number. A point at depth Z appears shifted between the left and right image by the disparity d; near things shift a lot, far things hardly at all. Your eyes, about 6.5 cm apart, do this all the time (binocular stereopsis). The ETH3D stereo rig used below has a baseline of 59.55 mm and, at the half resolution this page uses, a focal length of 271 pixels. Drag the point and change the baseline to see why stereo is precise up close and vague far away.

\[ d = x_L - x_R = \frac{f B}{Z} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Z = \frac{f B}{d} \]
Read it as: f is the focal length in pixels, B the baseline (distance between the camera centres), Z the depth. Similar triangles give the disparity: it is inversely proportional to depth. Double the distance, halve the disparity.
Say it“Disparity is f B over Z, so depth is f B over disparity.”
\[ \Delta Z \approx \Big|\frac{\partial Z}{\partial d}\Big| \Delta d = \frac{Z^2}{f B}\, \Delta d \]
Read it as: a matching error of Δd pixels moves the depth by about Z²Δd/(fB). The error grows with the square of the distance; a wider baseline or a longer focal length shrinks it.
Say it“Depth error is Z squared over f B, times the disparity error.”
disparity
depth Z
depth range for ±Δd

Now the real thing. To find a pixel’s match, compare a small window around it with windows on the same row of the other image, at every candidate disparity, and keep the best. The simplest cost is the sum of absolute differences (SAD). There is a catch on this real pair: the right camera exposed the scene darker (mean brightness 95.6 against 107.0), so raw brightness never matches. Subtracting each pixel’s local 5 × 5 mean first removes that offset. Click any pixel of the left image and read its cost curve; then switch the mean removal off.

\[ \begin{aligned} C(x,y,d) &= \frac{1}{(2r+1)^2}\sum_{|u|,|v| \le r} \big| \Delta_{uv} \big| \\ \Delta_{uv} &= L'(x{+}u,\,y{+}v) \\ &\quad - R'(x{+}u{-}d,\,y{+}v) \\ \hat d &= \arg\min_d C(x,y,d) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: L′ and R′ are the two images (after the optional mean removal); the window has radius r. Δuv compares one pixel of the window around (x, y) on the left with the pixel d places further left on the right image, and the cost averages the absolute differences over the window. The best d is the one with the lowest cost; fitting a parabola through the costs at d̂ − 1, d̂ and d̂ + 1 refines it to a fraction of a pixel.
Say it“The cost at disparity d is the mean absolute difference between the left window and the right window shifted by d; pick the d with the smallest cost.”
matched disparity
ground truth

Motion

A moving camera, and steering by sight

One camera that moves gives a second view for free: the next frame. As the camera travels forward, the image flows outward from a single point, the focus of expansion (FOE), which is exactly where the camera is heading. How fast a point flows depends on its depth: near things stream past, far things creep. So flow gives depth, though only up to the unknown speed: a world twice as large passed twice as fast looks the same. One quantity survives that ambiguity: the time to contact τ, the distance from a point to the FOE divided by how fast that distance grows. It tells you how many seconds until you reach a surface, with no idea of its size or your speed. Change the heading and click on points to read their τ.

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot x &= \frac{x V_z - f V_x}{Z} \\ \dot y &= \frac{y V_z - f V_y}{Z} \\ \text{FOE} &= \Big(\frac{f V_x}{V_z}, \frac{f V_y}{V_z}\Big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a camera translating with velocity (Vx, Vy, Vz) sees a point at image position (x, y), measured from the image centre, and depth Z move at this rate. The flow is zero at the FOE and points away from it; its size is proportional to 1/Z.
Say it“x-dot is x V-z minus f V-x, over Z; the focus of expansion is f V-x over V-z, f V-y over V-z.”
\[ \tau = \frac{Z}{V_z} = \frac{r}{\dot r} \]
Read it as: r is the image distance from a point to the FOE and ṙ how fast it grows. Their ratio equals depth over forward speed: the time to contact. It needs no calibration, no size and no speed, just two frames.
Say it“Tau is Z over V-z, which equals r over r-dot.”
FOE, pixels right of centre
τ = r / ṙ, clicked point
true Z / Vz

Controlling movement with vision. A vision system on a car, drone or robot arm exists to choose actions. One route is a pipeline: detect lanes and obstacles, rebuild the 3D scene, plan, act. The other learns the whole mapping from pixels to steering: ALVINN (Pomerleau, 1989) steered a van with a tiny network fed a 30 × 32 image, and NVIDIA’s PilotNet (Bojarski et al., 2016) did it with a CNN trained on human driving. Pipelines are easier to inspect and test; end-to-end systems need no hand-designed intermediate steps but fail in ways that are harder to predict. In between are control laws that act directly on an image measurement. Time to contact is the classic one (Lee, 1976): as you approach an obstacle its image width s grows, and τ = s/ṡ. To stop in time with braking strength amax you need a distance V²/(2amax), which works out to start braking once τ falls to V/(2amax). Set the speed and the trigger τ*, and add camera noise.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\hat\tau = \frac{s}{\dot s}, \quad \text{brake when } \hat\tau \le \tau^\ast \\ &\text{safe if } \tau^\ast \ge \frac{V}{2a_{\max}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the camera measures the obstacle’s width s in pixels in every frame; its growth rate ṡ comes from a finite difference over the last few frames. The car brakes at full strength amax = 7 m/s² once the estimate drops below the trigger τ*. Braking from speed V takes V²/(2amax) metres, and the car is τ*V metres away at the trigger, which gives the safety condition. Noise in s makes ṡ, and so τ̂, jumpy.
Say it“Tau-hat is s over s-dot; brake when it reaches tau-star; you stop in time if tau-star is at least V over two a-max.”
safe if τ* ≥
braking starts at
outcome

One image

Depth and size from a single view

Close one eye and the room does not go flat. A single image still carries depth cues: perspective (parallel lines meet at vanishing points), texture gradients (a tiled floor’s tiles shrink and squash with distance; a tile tilted away by a slant σ looks foreshortened by cos σ), shading (how brightness changes across a curved surface), contours and occlusion (whatever hides something else is in front), and familiar size (a person far away looks small, and we know people are not small). None of these is exact on its own; together, and with knowledge of what objects are like, they work well.

One of them gives real numbers. On a flat ground plane, the horizon is the image row where the ground meets infinity, and the lower an object’s foot appears below it, the nearer the object. For a camera held level at height hc, an object whose foot is at row yb and top at row yt has height hc(yb − yt)/(yb − yh), with no focal length needed (Hoiem, Efros & Hebert, 2006). Drag the horizon on this COCO photo until the players come out a believable size, or let the page fit it. Modern systems learn these cues from data instead: networks trained on images with measured depth predict a depth map from a single photo (Eigen et al., 2014), and others recover the 3D shape of objects from one picture.

\[ H = h_c\,\frac{y_b - y_t}{y_b - y_h}, \qquad Z = \frac{f\,h_c}{y_b - y_h} \]
Read it as: rows are counted downwards in pixels; yh is the horizon, yb the row of the object’s foot, yt the row of its top. The camera’s height hc sets the scale. An object whose foot sits close under the horizon is far away (the denominator is small), so the same pixel height means a taller object. The distance also needs f, but ratios of distances do not: they are just ratios of (yb − yh).
Say it“Height is camera height times the object's pixel height over the foot's distance below the horizon.”
horizon row yh
median height

Reconstruction

Many views: structure from motion

With dozens of photos of a scene, taken from places nobody measured, you can recover both the scene and where every photo was taken. This is structure from motion. Its steps: detect distinctive points in every image and match them across images; for a pair of images, estimate their relative pose from the matches (the epipolar constraint below, solved with as few as eight matches by Longuet-Higgins’ 1981 algorithm, inside RANSAC to survive bad matches); triangulate the matched points; add further images one at a time; and finally refine everything together by bundle adjustment (Triggs et al., 2000), named after the bundles of rays from each camera that it adjusts until they meet. Photo Tourism (Snavely, Seitz & Szeliski, 2006) rebuilt landmarks from tourists’ internet photos this way; multi-view stereo then fills in dense surfaces between the points.

The lab is a flatland version: a 2D world seen from above by cameras whose images are single rows of pixels. The cameras’ positions are only roughly known, as they would be from a phone’s sensors. Triangulating with those poses gives a distorted shape. Bundle adjustment then moves the cameras and the points to make every ray agree. The whole solution can still be shifted, turned or scaled without changing a single pixel (a gauge freedom), so the first camera is held fixed and so is the second camera’s x position, which sets the scale. Triangulate, then bundle-adjust; try two views versus eight, and a narrow arc versus a wide one.

\[ \mathbf x'^{\top} E\, \mathbf x = 0, \qquad E = [\mathbf t]_\times R \]
Read it as: x and x′ are the same scene point’s (calibrated) image positions in two views; R and t are the second camera’s rotation and translation relative to the first; [t]× is the matrix that takes a cross product with t. One matched pair gives one linear equation in the nine entries of E, so eight pairs fix it up to scale. Given x, the equation is a line in the other image: the epipolar line.
Say it“x-prime transpose E x equals zero, where E is t-cross times R.”
\[ \min_{\{C_j\},\{X_i\}} \sum_{(i,j)\,\text{seen}} \big\Vert\, u_{ij} - \pi(C_j, X_i)\, \big\Vert^2 \]
Read it as: Xi are the scene points, Cj the camera poses, uij where point i was observed in image j, and π projects a point into a camera. Bundle adjustment minimises the total squared reprojection error over all points and cameras together, usually with Levenberg–Marquardt, as here.
Say it“Minimise, over all cameras and points, the sum of squared distances between where each point was seen and where it projects.”

People

Understanding what people are doing

Many uses of vision are about people: is the pedestrian about to step out, is the patient getting up, which player has the ball? The usual first step is to find each person and their pose, the image positions of a fixed set of body keypoints (COCO uses 17: nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles). Networks predict a heat map per keypoint and read off its peak; bottom-up systems such as OpenPose (Cao et al., 2017) then group keypoints into people. Activities are harder. They are usually learned as classes of short video clips (Kinetics has 400 human actions) by networks that see both appearance and motion, for example a two-stream network with one stream on frames and one on optical flow (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014).

Why it is hard: one action looks very different from different viewpoints and people; different actions can look identical in a single frame (reaching for a cup or pushing it away); context matters (the same arm movement is waving on a platform and hailing on a kerb); and activities have different time scales, from a blink to a commute. Labels also leak: a classifier can “recognise” tennis from the court without looking at the player at all. To grade a predicted pose against a hand-labelled one, COCO uses object keypoint similarity, the IoU of poses. Add noise, drag keypoints, and compare a large person with a small one.

\[ \text{OKS} = \frac{\sum_i \exp\!\big(-d_i^2 / (2 s^2 \kappa_i^2)\big)\, [v_i > 0]}{\sum_i [v_i > 0]} \]
Read it as: di is the distance in pixels between predicted and true keypoint i; vi > 0 means the keypoint was labelled; s² is the person’s segmented area, so errors are measured relative to the person’s size; κi is a per-keypoint tolerance (twice COCO’s σi, which was measured from how much human annotators disagree: small for eyes, large for hips). Each keypoint scores between 0 and 1, and OKS is their average.
Say it“OKS is the average over labelled keypoints of e to the minus d squared over two s squared kappa squared.”

Vision and language

Linking pictures and words

Pictures and text meet in several tasks. Tagging attaches keywords to images. Captioning writes a sentence: “Show and tell” (Vinyals et al., 2015) fed a CNN’s image features into a recurrent language model. Visual question answering (Antol et al., 2015) answers a question about an image. And retrieval finds the image for a sentence, or the sentence for an image. The most influential recent approach, CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), trains an image encoder and a text encoder on 400 million image–caption pairs so that each image’s vector is closer to its own caption’s vector than to any other in the batch; the loss on the batch’s similarity matrix is shown below. Two cautions: captions describe what people found worth saying, not everything present; and a question-answering model can score well by guessing from the question alone (“what colour is the banana?”), so good benchmarks are built to block that.

This page cannot run CLIP, so it builds an honest, small, working version from pieces already on the page. The image encoder is YOLOX-Nano: an image becomes an 80-number vector holding the best detection score per COCO class. The text encoder is a word–category table learned from 22,514 COCO captions of 4,500 other images: how much more often a caption word appears with an object category than chance (positive PMI). A caption becomes the sum of its words’ rows. Pick a caption, or type your own, and see which of 100 held-out photos it retrieves.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{PMI}(w,c) &= \ln \frac{N\,(n_{wc} - \alpha)}{n_w\, n_c} \\ s(t, I) &= \cos\big(\mathbf q(t), \mathbf v(I)\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: N captions; nw contain word w; nc belong to images with an object of category c; nwc both. PMI is positive when w and c go together more than chance; the discount α damps pairs seen only a few times; negatives are set to 0. q(t) sums the rows of the caption’s words, v(I) is the image’s vector, and s is the cosine between them.
Say it“PMI is the log of N times the discounted joint count over the two single counts; similarity is the cosine of the caption and image vectors.”
\[ \mathcal L = -\frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln \frac{e^{\,s_{ii}/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\,s_{ij}/\tau}} \]
Read it as: sij is the similarity of caption i and image j; the matching pairs sit on the diagonal. Each row is a softmax over n images with temperature τ, and the loss is the average negative log probability of the right image. CLIP minimises this (and the same over columns) by training both encoders; here the encoders are fixed and the loss simply measures how well they line up.
Say it“The loss is minus the average log of e to the s-i-i over tau, over the sum across j of e to the s-i-j over tau.”

Real-world project

Project: grade a real detector, rebuild a real scene

Two real tasks with real data, both computed in your browser and checked against Python. First, the standard COCO evaluation of a published detector. YOLOX-Nano (Apache-2.0 licence) was run offline with ONNX Runtime on 500 photos drawn at random (seed 0) from COCO val2017, which it never trained on. The page holds its detections with score ≥ 0.05 after class-wise NMS (8,549 boxes) and the 3,542 hand-drawn boxes, and computes average precision exactly as the official pycocotools does: each detection is matched greedily, highest score first, to the best unmatched object of its class; precision is made non-increasing and read off at 101 recall levels; the result is averaged over the 80 classes and over IoU thresholds 0.50, 0.55, …, 0.95. COCO’s annotations are licensed CC BY 4.0.

Second, a 3D reconstruction from two photographs. The original idea was a scene from your own phone photos; this page uses a pair with a laser-scanned ground truth instead, so the result can be graded: ETH3D’s playground_1l (Schöps et al., 2017), licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The images were averaged down to half resolution (470 × 245) and embedded as lossless PNGs; the ground-truth disparity, kept only where it is valid and not occluded, is embedded to 1/20 pixel. The extract embedded in this page is shared under the same CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence.

Python, same settings

The same computations in Python

import json, re, io, base64, contextlib, numpy as np
from PIL import Image                                   # Pillow, only to decode the embedded PNGs
from pycocotools.coco import COCO                       # the official COCO evaluation code
from pycocotools.cocoeval import COCOeval
D = json.load(open("x059-coco.json")); ST = json.load(open("x059-stereo.json"))

# ---- 1. Score YOLOX-Nano's detections on 500 COCO val2017 images with the official tool
gt = {"images": [], "annotations": [], "categories": [{"id": c + 1} for c in range(80)]}
res = []
for iid, w, h, g, d in D["eval"]:
    gt["images"].append({"id": iid, "width": w, "height": h})
    for k in range(0, len(g), 7):
        gt["annotations"].append({"id": len(gt["annotations"]) + 1, "image_id": iid, "category_id": g[k] + 1,
                                  "bbox": g[k + 1:k + 5], "area": g[k + 5], "iscrowd": g[k + 6]})
    for k in range(0, len(d), 6):
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = d[k + 1:k + 5]
        res.append({"image_id": iid, "category_id": d[k] + 1, "bbox": [x1, y1, x2 - x1, y2 - y1], "score": d[k + 5]})
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    G = COCO(); G.dataset = gt; G.createIndex()
    E = COCOeval(G, G.loadRes(res), "bbox"); E.evaluate(); E.accumulate(); E.summarize()
s = E.stats
print(f"{len(D['eval'])} images, {len(gt['annotations'])} boxes ({sum(a['iscrowd'] for a in gt['annotations'])} crowd), {len(res)} detections with score >= 0.05")
print(f"AP[.5:.95] {s[0]:.6f}  AP50 {s[1]:.4f}  AP75 {s[2]:.4f}  AP small {s[3]:.4f}  medium {s[4]:.4f}  large {s[5]:.4f}")
pc = E.eval["precision"][:, :, :, 0, 2]                 # IoU x recall x category, area all, 100 detections
ap = [pc[:, :, c][pc[:, :, c] > -1].mean() if (pc[:, :, c] > -1).any() else None for c in range(80)]
best = sorted((a, D["cats"][c]) for c, a in enumerate(ap) if a is not None)
print("weakest:", ", ".join(f"{n} {a:.3f}" for a, n in best[:3]), "| strongest:", ", ".join(f"{n} {a:.3f}" for a, n in best[-3:]))

# ---- 2. Stereo: SAD block matching on the ETH3D pair, scored against the ground truth
dec = lambda b: np.array(Image.open(io.BytesIO(base64.b64decode(b))), dtype=np.float64)
L0, R0, GT = dec(ST["L"]), dec(ST["R"]), dec(ST["G"]); h, w = L0.shape; gd = GT / 20; ok = GT > 0
def prefilter(A, r):                                    # (2r+1)^2 * A - local window sum, edges repeated: A minus its local mean, scaled to stay integer
    k = 2 * r + 1; I = np.zeros((h + k, w + k)); I[1:, 1:] = np.pad(A, r, mode="edge").cumsum(0).cumsum(1)
    return k * k * A - (I[k:, k:] - I[:-k, k:] - I[k:, :-k] + I[:-k, :-k])
def match(rad, pre=2, dmax=16, sub=True):
    L, R, sc = (prefilter(L0, pre), prefilter(R0, pre), (2 * pre + 1) ** 2) if pre else (L0, R0, 1)
    vol = np.full((dmax + 1, h, w), np.inf)
    for d in range(dmax + 1):
        ad = np.full((h, w), 255.0); ad[:, d:] = np.abs(L[:, d:] - R[:, :w - d])
        I = np.zeros((h + 1, w + 1)); I[1:, 1:] = ad.cumsum(0).cumsum(1); k = 2 * rad + 1
        box = (I[k:, k:] - I[:-k, k:] - I[k:, :-k] + I[:-k, :-k]) / (k ** 2 * sc)
        vol[d, rad:h - rad, rad + d:w - rad] = box[:, d:]
    b = vol.argmin(0); bc = vol.min(0); disp = b.astype(float)
    if sub:
        inner = (b > 0) & (b < dmax); bi = np.clip(b, 1, dmax - 1)
        cm = np.take_along_axis(vol, (bi - 1)[None], 0)[0]; cp = np.take_along_axis(vol, (bi + 1)[None], 0)[0]
        den = cm - 2 * bc + cp; use = inner & np.isfinite(den) & (den > 0)
        disp[use] += 0.5 * (cm - cp)[use] / den[use]
    disp[~np.isfinite(bc)] = np.nan
    v = ok & np.isfinite(disp); e = np.abs(disp - gd)[v]
    return disp, v.sum() / ok.sum(), (e > 1).mean(), e.mean()
print(f"stereo pair {w} x {h}, {ok.sum()} pixels with ground truth, f = {ST['f']:.2f} px, baseline {ST['B']:.2f} mm")
print(f"  mean brightness: left {L0.mean():.2f}, right {R0.mean():.2f}")
print("  window   raw SAD: matched  bad>1px  mean|err|   local mean removed: matched  bad>1px  mean|err|")
PYST = {}
for rad in range(1, 8):
    a, b = match(rad, 0)[1:], match(rad, 2)[1:]; PYST[rad] = [list(a), list(b)]
    print(f"  {2 * rad + 1:2d} x {2 * rad + 1:<2d}  {a[0]:12.4f} {a[1]:8.4f} {a[2]:9.4f}   {b[0]:27.4f} {b[1]:8.4f} {b[2]:9.4f}")
disp = match(3)[0]; Z = ST["f"] * ST["B"] / disp[ok & (disp > 0.5)] / 1000
print(f"  7 x 7 depths: median {np.median(Z):.3f} m, 5th-95th percentile {np.percentile(Z, 5):.3f}-{np.percentile(Z, 95):.3f} m")

# ---- 3. Pictures and words: rank 100 images for each caption with a PMI word-category table
W = D["words"]; stop = set(W["stop"]); vi = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(W["vocab"])}
def toks(t):
    out = []
    for x in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", t.lower()):
        if x in stop or len(x) < 3: continue
        out.append(x[:-1] if len(x) > 3 and x.endswith("s") and not x.endswith("ss") else x)
    return out
def table(alpha):
    T = np.zeros((len(W["vocab"]), 80)); t = np.array(W["trip"]).reshape(-1, 3)
    n = t[:, 2] - alpha; v = np.log(W["N"] * np.maximum(n, 1e-300) / (np.array(W["nw"])[t[:, 0]] * np.array(W["nc"])[t[:, 1]]))
    keep = (n > 0) & (v > 0); T[t[keep, 0], t[keep, 1]] = v[keep]; return T
ev = {e[0]: e for e in D["eval"]}
def image_vecs(kind, smin):
    V = np.zeros((len(W["test"]), 80))
    for r, iid in enumerate(W["test"]):
        g, d = ev[iid][3], ev[iid][4]
        if kind == "gt":
            for k in range(0, len(g), 7):
                if not g[k + 6]: V[r, g[k]] = 1
        else:
            for k in range(0, len(d), 6):
                if d[k + 5] >= smin: V[r, d[k]] = max(V[r, d[k]], d[k + 5])
    return V
def retrieval(alpha, kind, smin):
    T = table(alpha); Q = np.array([sum((T[vi[x]] for x in set(toks(c)) if x in vi), np.zeros(80)) for c in W["caps"]])
    V = image_vecs(kind, smin); nq = np.linalg.norm(Q, axis=1, keepdims=True); nv = np.linalg.norm(V, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    Sim = np.where((nq > 0) & (nv.T > 0), Q @ V.T / np.maximum(nq * nv.T, 1e-300), 0)
    rank = np.array([1 + np.sum(Sim[i] > Sim[i, i] + 1e-12) + np.sum(np.abs(Sim[i, :i] - Sim[i, i]) <= 1e-12) for i in range(len(Sim))])
    return rank, Sim
PYW = {}
for kind, smin in (("det", 0.3), ("gt", 0)):
    rank, Sim = retrieval(2, kind, smin)
    lg = Sim / 0.1; lg -= lg.max(1, keepdims=True); nll = -(np.diag(lg) - np.log(np.exp(lg).sum(1))).mean()
    PYW[kind] = [float(np.mean(rank <= 1)), float(np.mean(rank <= 5)), float(nll)]
    print(f"captions -> images ({'detector, score >= 0.3' if kind == 'det' else 'true COCO labels'}): R@1 {np.mean(rank <= 1):.2f}  R@5 {np.mean(rank <= 5):.2f}  median rank {np.median(rank):.1f}  InfoNCE loss (tau 0.1) {nll:.4f}")
print(f"PMI table: {len(W['vocab'])} words x 80 categories from {W['N']} captions of 4,500 other val2017 images")
json.dump({"ap": list(s[:6]), "st": PYST, "w": PYW}, open("x059-py.json", "w"))   # the page's comparison column

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A detector returns (class, box, score) for every object. Boxes are graded by IoU; a detector is graded by average precision, averaged over classes and (in COCO) over IoU thresholds 0.5 to 0.95.
  • Two-stage detectors propose regions (learned from anchors in Faster R-CNN) and then classify and refine them; one-stage detectors predict a box at every grid cell in one pass. Both need non-maximum suppression to remove duplicates.
  • Two views give depth by triangulation: Z = fB/d. The hard part is correspondence; the epipolar constraint turns the search into a line, and the depth error grows with Z².
  • Motion, many photos and even one photo carry 3D information: flow radiates from the focus of expansion and gives time to contact; structure from motion and bundle adjustment recover cameras and scene together; the horizon and familiar sizes give scale in a single view.
  • Applications chain these pieces: poses for understanding people (graded by OKS), shared image–text embeddings for captions and retrieval, and image measurements fed straight into control, like braking on τ.

Check your understanding

A 20 × 20-pixel box and a 200 × 200-pixel box are each predicted 5 pixels too far to the right. Which loses more IoU, and why does that matter for small objects?

The small one: the 5-pixel strip is a quarter of its width, so its IoU falls to 15/25 = 0.6, while the large box keeps 195/205 ≈ 0.95. Small objects therefore fail strict IoU thresholds far more often, which is one reason COCO’s AP for small objects is so much lower.

Why does a one-stage detector need NMS, and what goes wrong if θ is set too low?

Neighbouring cells and grids all see the same object and each predicts a box for it, so one object yields a cluster of near-duplicate boxes; NMS keeps the best of each cluster. With a low θ, a correct box for a second object that overlaps the first (people standing close) is deleted as a duplicate, so recall drops.

A stereo rig has f = 800 px and B = 0.12 m. What is the depth error for a 0.5-pixel matching error at 4 m and at 40 m?

ΔZ ≈ Z²Δd/(fB) = 16 × 0.5/96 ≈ 0.083 m at 4 m, and 1600 × 0.5/96 ≈ 8.3 m at 40 m: a hundred times worse for ten times the distance.

Why can a single moving camera measure time to contact but not distance?

Flow depends on depth divided by speed: doubling both the scene’s size and the speed gives the same images. Their ratio, Z/Vz = τ, is exactly what the images fix, so τ = r/ṙ is measurable while Z alone is not, unless the speed or an object’s size is known.

Bundle adjustment reaches a reprojection error of 0.5 px, yet the reconstruction is twice as big as the real scene. Has it failed?

No. Images alone cannot fix the overall position, orientation and scale of the scene (the gauge freedom): a twice-as-large scene seen by cameras twice as far apart gives identical images. Metric scale needs one known distance, such as a known baseline or a GPS track.
